summary: A landlocked country in Eastern Europe that was once part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, was later absorbed into the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union, became independent in 1991, and maintains close ties with Russia.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: Eastern Orthodoxy arrived with the baptism of Grand Prince Vladimir of Kievan Rus' in 988, and a bishopric had already been established at Polotsk by 992. From the 14th century Belarus was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, and Catholic influence expanded; after the Third Partition of Poland in 1795, Belarus came under the Russian Empire, and in 1839 the tsarist government forced Eastern-rite Catholics to merge into the Russian Orthodox Church, making Orthodoxy the majority religion.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism arrived after the Grand Duchy of Lithuania converted to Catholicism (1387) in the 14th century, and during the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth it spread among the nobility and in the western regions. Today's Catholics are mainly Poles and Belarusians in the Grodno region of the west, which belonged to Poland from 1921 to 1939, so the Catholic tradition there is deeper.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population stems from the atheist policies pursued during Soviet rule from 1919 to 1991, when large numbers of churches were closed or demolished and religious education was interrupted. Although there was a religious revival after independence, about one in ten people still do not identify with any religion, and the proportion actually taking part in religious activities is also quite low.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism was popular among the nobility of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania during the 16th-century Reformation; for example, the Radziwiłł family supported Calvinism, but it later declined during the Counter-Reformation. Today's Protestants are mainly Baptists and Pentecostals, who grew through underground churches and international missionary work in the late Soviet period and after independence, but they remain under strict government control.

religion.background: Belarus accepted Eastern Orthodoxy after the baptism of Kievan Rus' in 988, and the Principality of Polotsk was an early center of Orthodoxy. From the 14th century it was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and the later Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth caused Catholicism and the Eastern-rite Catholic Church, created by the 1596 Union of Brest, to expand there. After its incorporation into the Russian Empire in 1795, the tsars pursued Russification and abolished the Eastern-rite Catholic Church in 1839. Judaism was also very important in Belarus; in the early 20th century about half the residents of cities such as Minsk were Jewish, but the Nazi Holocaust of 1941–1944 almost destroyed the Jewish community. The atheist policies of the Soviet era devastated all religions, and after independence in 1991 Orthodoxy regained its dominant position.

language.official: The official languages are Belarusian and Russian.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Russian became the administrative language after Belarus was incorporated into the Russian Empire in 1795, and it was promoted even more vigorously in the Soviet era; urbanization and industrialization led large numbers of peasants to move to cities such as Minsk and switch to speaking Russian. In 1995 President Lukashenko held a referendum that made Russian an official language equal to Belarusian, and since then Russian has been overwhelmingly dominant in government, media and education, with about 70% of the population using Russian daily.

ranking.name: Belarusian
ranking.description: Belarusian is an East Slavic language, close to Russian and Ukrainian. From the 14th to 16th centuries Ruthenian, which was based on Old Belarusian, was the official language of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and the Lithuanian Statute of 1588 was written in this language. But under the Russification policies of the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union it gradually retreated to the countryside. In the early 1990s it was the sole official language, but after 1995 its status declined; although many people give it as their mother tongue in censuses, relatively few use it in daily life.

language.history: Belarusian descends from East Slavic and, in the form of Ruthenian, became the official and legal language of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the 14th–17th centuries. In 1696 the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth made Polish its official language, and the status of Belarusian declined; after its incorporation into the Russian Empire in 1795, and especially after the failure of the 1863 uprising, the empire restricted Belarusian publishing more strictly. The 'Belarusization' policy of the early Soviet period in the 1920s promoted Belarusian, but from the 1930s the policy turned to large-scale Russification, and many Belarusian-speaking intellectuals were executed in 1937. The 1995 referendum made Russian one of the official languages, and the use of Belarusian has continued to decline.

ranking.name: Draniki (potato pancakes)
ranking.description: Potatoes are grated into a fine pulp, mixed with onion and a little flour or egg, and fried in a pan into golden thin pancakes, often eaten with sour cream.
ranking.history: Potatoes became widespread in Belarus only in the late 18th century; suited to the cool, damp climate and sandy soil, they quickly became the peasants' staple, and Belarusians were even nicknamed 'potato people' (bulbashi). The earliest recipes for draniki appeared in the 19th century, and the dish is regarded as the national dish of Belarus. Some cities even hold annual festivals themed on draniki.

ranking.name: Khaladnik (cold beet soup)
ranking.description: A chilled pink soup made from a beet broth base with chopped cucumber, boiled eggs, dill and sour cream, served cold.
ranking.history: Cold beet soup is a summer dish shared by Belarus, Lithuania and Poland, reflecting the food culture these regions shared during the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. Beets are a hardy crop common in Eastern Europe that can be stored through the winter and, in summer, are made into a refreshing cold soup. In the hot summer, this pink soup is the most common cooling dish on Belarusian family tables.

ranking.name: Kalduny (potato dumplings)
ranking.description: Dumplings with a wrapper of mashed potato or flour, filled with pork, mushrooms or cheese, boiled or fried and eaten with sour cream or fried bacon bits, with a hearty texture.
ranking.history: Kalduny are common in Belarus, Lithuania and Poland, and the name is generally thought to be borrowed from a Turkic language, reflecting exchanges with Tatars and other eastern peoples in the era of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Belarusians often use mashed potato instead of flour for the wrapper, showing the country's reliance on the potato. It is a common dish at winter family gatherings and a signature dish in traditional restaurants.

ranking.name: Babka (potato bake)
ranking.description: Grated potatoes are mixed with bacon and onion and baked in the oven, giving a crisp, browned exterior and a soft interior, like a savory potato cake.
ranking.history: Potato babka is popular in both Belarus and Lithuania; the name 'babka' means 'grandmother', because its shape resembles a traditional tall cylindrical cake. It is a country dish that developed after the potato became widespread from the 19th century on, and was traditionally baked for hours in a wood-fired oven. Today it is a classic dish at Belarusian family weekends and festivals, and a representative showcase of Belarus's 'potato culture'.

ranking.name: Kvass
ranking.description: A low-alcohol drink made by fermenting rye bread or malt with water, with a slight sourness and a caramel-like bread aroma, served chilled, with a refreshing, mildly sweet taste.
ranking.history: Kvass has a history of more than a thousand years among the East Slavs and is already recorded in the Kievan Rus' chronicles of the 10th century. It is fermented from dried rye bread, showing the peasants' habit of valuing food. In the Soviet era, yellow barrel trucks selling kvass were a common sight on the streets, becoming a childhood memory for many. Today it remains the most popular traditional summer drink in Belarus.
